description: Somos un grupo de mujeres de la Universidad Escuela Colombiana de Ingeniería Julio Garavito.
summary:
ANDROMEDA is a space-themed video game in which anyone can complete beginner, intermediate, and advanced space missions. Each player chooses a mission, equips their spacecraft, navigates a maze in search of the necessary scientific instruments, and carries out the mission with limited resources. If resources run low, players can replenish them by answering questions about real life space missions.
The challenge involves a game where users plan and carry out their own mission. ANDROMEDA translates this into concrete decisions: designing the spacecraft, selecting instruments, and managing energy and time. In this way, players face the trade-offs involved in designing space missions.
It brings aerospace engineering to everyone no expertise required through an intuitive interface and a fun challenge. It teaches that efficient use of resources is key to a mission’s success and leaves players curious to keep learning.
details:
ANDROMEDA is an educational browser game in which players design and run space missions the way real mission teams do: by choosing, preparing and managing limited resources. The player selects a level (Beginner – CubeSat, Intermediate – James Webb Space Telescope, Advanced – SLS / Artemis II), assembles the spacecraft in a timed puzzle, crosses a generated maze to collect the tools the mission requires, and then completes a scientific mission guided by Laika, our astronaut-dog mascot (Inspired on the real Laika). Every mission ends with a 100-point evaluation and feedback, so players can retry and improve.

We developed four missions across the three levels:

Wildfire detection (CubeSat): the player locates a forest fire on a grid map using a multispectral camera and an infrared thermal sensor, interprets the data, and transmits a report to the ground station.

Space environment characterization (CubeSat): the player responds to a solar-activity alert, reads particle, radiation, temperature and magnetic-field data, and chooses shielding measures to protect the satellite.

James Webb Space Telescope: the player picks an astronomical target (galaxy, exoplanet or star-forming region), points the telescope with the fine guidance sensor, protects it with the sunshield, chooses the right instrument (NIRCam, NIRSpec or MIRI), and builds a scientific report.

Artemis II (Advanced level): the player commands a crewed mission around the Moon aboard the Orion spacecraft, responsible for the safety of four astronauts from launch to splashdown.

Across all missions, players manage limited resources, such as energy and protection levels, that their decisions consume, so every action has a cost.

Advanced level – Artemis II. The Advanced level takes players through a full lunar flyby in six events: preparation and launch, Earth-orbit systems checks, the trajectory to the Moon, the lunar flyby and surface observation, the return and splashdown, and continuous resource management and emergency response. Players inspect systems, supervise navigation, observe lunar features with high-resolution cameras, handle alerts such as oxygen drops or power failures, and manage oxygen, water, food, energy and fuel throughout the journey. The mission is scored out of 100 points: crew safety (30), resource management (25), emergency resolution (25) and mission objectives (20). The player wins by completing the lunar flyby and returning all four astronauts safely to Earth.

Benefits and intended impact. The game introduces students to remote sensing, space weather, infrared astronomy and human spaceflight in an engaging, low-pressure format. Players learn that space missions serve both Earth and the universe, and that real missions involve trade-offs such as limited resources, instrument selection, risk protection and crew safety. It runs in any modern browser with no installation, works offline, and its interface is currently in Spanish to reach Spanish-speaking students.

Tools and technologies. We built the game with HTML5, CSS3 and vanilla JavaScript (ES6 modules, no external frameworks); original SVG graphics for spacecraft, planets and the mascot; browser localStorage to save progress, levels and best scores; a procedural maze generator that guarantees every maze is solvable and every tool reachable; and the Node.js built-in test runner (8 automated tests covering level timing, scoring, game flow and maze logic, all passing). We developed and tested the project with Visual Studio Code, using Live Server or Python’s local HTTP server, and used optional Google Fonts (Nunito, Orbitron) with local fallback fonts. All mission parameters and scoring rules come from our own design documents.

Use of artificial intelligence. The code of this project was developed with the support of artificial intelligence, specifically ChatGPT-6. Our team designed the game concept, levels, missions, scoring rules and educational content in written specification documents, and ChatGPT-6 generated and repaired the code from those specifications. We then reviewed, tested and corrected the results ourselves.

What makes it creative. Instead of a quiz, learning happens through play: we turned assembling a spacecraft into a puzzle, collecting tools into a maze, and mission operations into decisions with real consequences. A friendly astronaut-dog character guides players, and each mission combines planning, exploration and scientific interpretation.

Factors our team considered. We balanced scientific accuracy against simplicity for young learners, used clear, age-appropriate language, and made limited resources the core mechanic. We also made scoring fair, so every mission totals exactly 100 points, and designed for offline use, low hardware requirements and accessibility (keyboard, touch and screen-reader labels). Finally, we documented every design assumption, and all visuals and data are educational simulations, not real NASA measurements.
